reason: Moving a fixed clock: Playwright's fastForward advances a fixed clock's timers while its wall time stays put. Strider's adjust refuses a fixed clock (WrongMode), and its setTime changes a fixed clock's wall time, so a fixed clock can't be moved without changing the time it shows. The matrix row says fastForward is present as setTime, which holds for controlled clocks only

Running timers under a fixed clock: Playwright's runFor(0) fires the timers set under a fixed time. Strider's adjust refuses a fixed clock (WrongMode), and a fixed clock's timers are real ones that run in real time, so the test can't be expressed. The matrix row says runFor is present, which holds for controlled clocks only

runFor on a clock that runs in real time: Playwright's runFor advances a flowing clock, which then keeps flowing. Strider's adjust refuses a clock that runs in real time (WrongMode), and resume is one way, so a controlled clock from 0 would give exactly 10000 without the running time the test bounds. The matrix row says runFor is present, which holds for controlled clocks only

fastForward on a clock that runs in real time: Playwright's fastForward jumps a flowing clock, which then keeps flowing. Strider's setTime refuses a clock that runs in real time (WrongMode), and resume is one way, so a controlled clock from 0 would give exactly 10000 without the running time the test bounds. The matrix row says fastForward is present as setTime, which holds for controlled and fixed clocks only

Pausing a clock that runs in real time: Playwright's pauseAt stops a flowing clock at a time. Strider's resume turns a clock into a real-time one for good, and a controlled clock never runs, so there is no running clock to pause; a controlled clock that stays put would pass the test without ever having run
